pages.text: Connected pipes and fittings make one $(thing)network$(): a single volume at a single pressure. A pipe has a bore of 100 mm, about 8 litres to the metre. Gas obeys $(bold)pV = nRT$(), so its pressure follows its absolute temperature. Liquid weighs: a column of water presses on its foot with 1 atm for each 10 m. How fast anything flows follows Darcy and Weisbach: a long rough pipe passes less.$(br2)A network bursts at its weakest wall or joint, and breaking a pipe lets out everything in the run. Close a valve first.
pages.title: A run of pipe

pages.text: Three lumber or three fire bricks make three pipes of wood or fired clay. Two sheets of copper, lead, wrought iron or steel make two pipes of that metal.

Barlow's formula gives the bursting pressure of a thin wall: p = 2 S t / D.$(li)wood 8.9 atm, to 177 °C$(li)fired clay 3.5 atm, to 1127 °C$(li)copper 10 atm, to 427 °C$(li)lead 5.9 atm, to 150 °C$(li)wrought iron 10 atm, to 627 °C$(li)steel 10 atm, to 727 °C$(br)Joints of hemp and tallow hold 10 atm at most, whatever the metal: steel gains nothing over iron until rubber gaskets come. Hotter than its limit a pipe holds nothing.
pages.title: What a wall holds

pages.text: Heat a closed pipe and its gas gains pressure with the absolute temperature. Water adds the pressure of its vapour (the Antoine equation): 1 atm at 100 °C, 4.7 at 150 °C and 10 at 180 °C, which is the limit of the joints.$(br2)Worst is a pipe filled to the brim with liquid. Water expands 0.021% a kelvin and is hardly compressible, so each kelvin of warming adds 4.6 atm: two kelvin burst an iron pipe at once. Leave room for the liquid to expand, or fit a safety valve.
pages.title: Heat, steam and water

pages.text: The $(thing)Pressure Vessel$() is eight wrought iron double sheets round a hollow: half a cubic metre that joins every pipe touching it.

A fire below a pressure vessel heats the whole network joined to it, and a vessel with water and a closed outlet is a boiler. Its pressure climbs with the temperature until something gives way. Nothing makes it safe but a $(thing)safety valve$() and a hand to watch the gauge.$(br2)Its walls count as a pipe's do: Barlow, the joints, the temperature limit and the corrosion of what it holds. See $(l:tfcpp/pipes#walls)the table$().
pages.title: Boilers

pages.text: The $(thing)Safety Valve$() is three ingots under a brass mechanism: wrought iron, or lead. A fired clay one is made of fire bricks.

A valve has to lift before its own body gives way, so its weight is set to four fifths of the rating of the body, up to 8 atm. An iron one lifts at 8 atm above the air outside and seats again at 7, with a loud hiss; one of lead lifts at 4.7 and seats at 3.7; one of fired clay at 2.8, seat 1.8. It cannot be held shut.$(br2)Drowned in liquid, it still lifts, and the gas bubbles out through the liquid. The hiss tells you that the pressure is high.
pages.title: The safety valve

pages.text: $(li)$(thing)Gate valve$(): a hand wheel. Closed, it splits the network in two. It cannot be turned again for a second.$(li)$(thing)Vent$(): an open pipe end that passes gas either way, by the pressure on each side. Into liquid it lets gas only out.$(li)$(thing)Tap$(): lets liquid out into a barrel or any holder in front of it.$(br)Each comes in iron, lead and fired clay, and takes the strength and the corrosion of its body. Two liquids never join: pipes that carry them touch without opening to each other.
pages.title: Fittings

pages.text: The $(thing)Piston Pump$() is three wrought iron double sheets under a brass mechanism. A shaft drives it from the side.

The pump takes in from its back (a pipe, a barrel, standing water or the air) and delivers into a pipe at its front. Each turn sweeps 20 litres, and the shaft pays for the pressure difference and the lift of the liquid in the front pipe.$(br2)The air pushes water up a suction pipe 10.3 m at most, acid of density 1800 only 5.7 m. A pump takes no lava or molten metal, and delivers into no line that runs on into unloaded land. Right-click it to see why it stands. See $(l:mechanics/pumps)Pumps$().
pages.title: The pump

pages.text: A burst frees the energy of the gas as it expands to the air, and of the hot water that flashes to steam. A vessel of 500 litres of water at 180 °C gives about 28 MJ. The shock works as a gas blast does (see $(l:tfcpp/mine_safety#blast)Mine Safety$()), and steam scalds everyone within four blocks.$(br2)Liquid of a thousand litres or more spills as blocks, and any corrosive liquid splashes the people near. A pipe whose wall has lost more than a twentieth gives nothing back when you pick it up.
pages.title: When it bursts

pages.text: The $(thing)Mercury Manometer$() is glass panes round a bulb of mercury, from $(l:tfcpp/sulfides#mercury)cinnabar$().

Right-click it to read the pressure in millimetres of mercury: 760 is the air outside. It also says when the line runs on past loaded land.$(br2)Above 3 atm over the air outside the mercury is blown out of the tube into the room, once (and mercury is poison: see $(l:tfcpp/poisons#mercury)Poisons$()). The tube then leaks a hundredth of the bore, and the pipes keep their pressure otherwise.
pages.title: Reading the gauge

pages.text: Corrosion eats a share of the wall each process day (24 minutes) in a full pipe. Iron or steel, copper, lead, wood:$(li)$(l:tfcpp/acids#tank)chamber acid$(): 0.5, 0.2, 0.001, 0.5$(li)sulfuric acid: 0.01, 0.1, 0.1, 1.0$(li)nitric acid: 0.02, 2.0, 0.5, 1.0$(li)hydrochloric acid: 2.0, 0.1, 0.1, 0.02$(br)Fired clay takes none of these. Strong acid passivates iron, but dilute eats it, and chloride never lets it. Lead holds sulfuric acid under a film of sulfate until 80 °C, then loses 20 times faster.
pages.title: Corrosion by liquids

pages.text: Per process day, in a full pipe:$(li)mercury in copper: 1.0 (iron flasks carried it)$(li)vinegar: lead 0.1, iron and copper 0.05$(li)brine: iron 0.03, copper 0.005$(li)water: iron 0.002$(li)hot lye above 80 °C: fired clay 0.05$(br)In pure gas: sulfur dioxide takes 0.1 from iron and nothing from lead, whose film it feeds. Ammonia takes 0.5 from copper, chlorine 0.3.$(br2)A worn wall bursts: look at your pipes.
pages.title: Other corrosion

pages.text: A network is worked out while its chunks are loaded. A run that ends in unloaded land is marked as running on: the pump will not deliver into it, and the gauge says so. A liquid that has overflowed is kept until it makes a whole block, and does not vanish.$(br2)Corrosion is counted for each section of pipe from when it was last looked at, so a section left in unloaded land for days pays for them all when it returns.
pages.title: Loaded land
